articles.title: LPGA Tour: England's Lottie Woad withdraws mid-round with illness as Yuna Nishimura wins Walmart NW Arkansas Championship
articles.summary: Lottie Woad withdrew from the Walmart NW Arkansas Championship during her final round; Yuna Nishimura closed out a wire-to-wire victory and maiden LPGA Tour title; two players carded holes-in-one during the final day
articles.body:
Nishimura took a five-shot lead into the final day at Pinnacle Country Club, where she followed back-to-back 63s with a five-under 66 to close out a five-stroke victory.

The 26-year-old eagled the par-five 14th and mixed five birdies with two bogeys over the rest of her round, pulling her clear of Aki Iwai, Chanettee Wannasaen, and In Gee Chun in tied-second.

"A five-shot lead is a pretty tough situation, but I believed in myself and just kept going until the end," Nishimura said. "I missed a lot of cuts this year, so for me to win this tournament is a surprise, but it's a dream come true."

Iwai had closed on the lead after six birdies in seven holes during a bogey-free 62, with Wannasaen (64) and Chun (65) the others on 16 under, with England's Jodi Ewart Shadoff a further stroke back in a share of fifth after three consecutive 66s.

Yealimi Noh aced the par-three 15th hole with a nine-iron from 136 yards, the first of her LPGA Tour career, while Mao Saigo holed a seven-iron from 159 yards on the par-three third.

Woad started the day six shots off the lead and was five over for her round when she withdrew due to illness, shortly after hitting her drive out of bounds at the par-five 14th.

Her Solheim Cup teammate Julia Lopez Ramirez finished seven strokes adrift in a share of eighth, as Charley Hull faded to a tied-22nd finish after a final-round 70.

Alexandra extends LET Order of Merit lead with Italian title

South Africa's Casandra Alexander secured her third Ladies European Tour title - and second in a month - after completing a three-shot victory at the Buccellati Ladies Italian Open.

Alexander, who is also a five-time runner-up on the LET this season, posted a three-under 69 on the final day at Golf Club Milano to pull clear of Germany's Sophie Hausmann and American rookie Anna Morgan.

The 27-year-old card an eagle, four birdies, a bogey and a double-bogey during her eventful final round, with victory following on from last month's success at the KPMG Women's Irish Open.

"I'm glad I didn't have to wait for this one as long as I waited for the previous one," said Alexander. "My game's in the right place to win golf tournaments, so I'm looking forward to the rest of the season and having more opportunities."

Alexander started the final day tied for the lead and recovered from being four behind after five holes to pull level with an eagle at the par-five ninth. She added three birdies in the last four holes to pull away from the field.

Victory strengthens Alexander's position at the top of the LET Order of Merit, where she now extends her advantage over Anna Huang heading into the final stretch of the season.

articles.title: Scottie Scheffler's classy move offsets gallery shouting at Presidents Cup
articles.summary: Scottie Scheffler had a moment of notable sportsmanship on Sunday at the Presidents Cup.
articles.body:
American golf galleries are embarrassing themselves these days. Between harassing the European Ryder Cup team last year and actively rooting against Wyndham Clark at the U.S. Open this year , loudmouths in galleries are staining many of golf's finest events.

Sunday at the Presidents Cup at Medinah Country Club outside Chicago, Scottie Scheffler and Nico Echavarria of Colombia were late in their singles match. Scheffler was 3-up on Echavarria with five holes to play … and Scheffler also happens to be ranked No. 1 in the world, while Echavarria is ranked 61st. This wasn't exactly a fair fight.

That didn't stop someone in the gallery from elbowing their way into the match. As Echavarria teed off on the 14th hole, someone shouted "Go Scottie!" in his backswing. Echavarria dropped his club, and Scheffler immediately barked at the offender, saying, "There's no place for that."

"It's just ridiculous, somebody yelling in his swing off the tee," Scheffler said after the match. "There's absolutely no place for that. You should get 30 seconds to a minute when you're over the ball or getting ready to hit your shot where there's some silence, and it's just frustrating."

Up on the 14th green after the shout, Scheffler conceded a 32-foot par putt to Echavarria, a classy gesture that seemed as much an apology for the fan's behavior as anything else. Scheffler would go on to win the match 2&1, helping the United States attempt to rally back from a historic deficit.

"To be honest with you, I don't even really want to talk about it," Scheffler said afterward. "I think there's no real place for that in our game. I think we just leave it at that."

Fair enough, and that's probably the right thing to do. That, and eject screaming gallery idiots into the parking lot.

articles.title: Presidents Cup: Scottie Scheffler calls out heckler behaviour and is praised for 'amazing' sportsmanship in singles win
articles.summary: Nico Echavarria was disrupted by a spectator during a backswing in his Sunday singles defeat to Scottie Scheffler, who conceded a lengthy putt on the hole because of the incident; Scheffler claimed a 2&1 win as Team USA produced a 17-13 comeback victory over the International Team
articles.body:
The world No 1 faced Nico Echavarria on the final day at Medinah, where the Colombian was distracted by a spectator yelling in his backswing during his tee shot at the par-four 14th.

Echavarria dropped his club and stared at the culprit as his ball finished in the right rough, while Scheffler called out the heckler. The Presidents Cup rookie then had to lay up and failed to stay on the green with his third shot.

Scheffler generously conceded his opponent's 32-foot putt for par because of the incident, extending the match, before closing out a 2&1 win to move the United States a point closer to their victory target.

"To be honest with you, I don't even really want to talk about it," Scheffler told Golf Channel after his win. "I think there's no real place for that in our game."

American fans were accused of "crossing the line" during last year's Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black, where European players were subjected to personal abuse, although there have been far less crowd issues during the Presidents Cup.

"It's just ridiculous, somebody yelling in his swing off the tee," Scheffler added. "You should get 30 seconds to a minute when you're over the ball, or getting ready to hit your shot, where there's some silence. It's just frustrating."

Echavarria made par at the 15th and extended the match with a stunning chip-in birdie from off the 16th green, where he shushed the home crowd in celebration, before seeing his defeat confirmed on the next hole.

"What happened on 14 with that fan was very unfortunate," Echavarria admitted. "But he [Scheffler] gave me a 20-footer for par, which shows the character of the No 1 in the world.

"He is just different. He's a good person overall. Even with how good he is [as a player], he's a truly amazing guy. I wish it would have gone to the 18th, but he played well."

On the chip-in at the 16th, Echavarria added: "It's just frustrating with the amount of things that they say to you, so when you can give one back to them, it feels really good. Making that to keep the match going was very cool."

Scheffler's victory was one of 9.5 points won by Team USA on a record-breaking final day in Chicago, completing a 17-13 victory and the biggest final-day comeback in Presidents Cup history, with International Team captain Geoff Ogilvy joining the world No 1 in condoning the mid-swing yelling.

"I think for the most part out there it [the atmosphere] was great," Ogilvy said in his press conference, having fallen short in their bid for a first Presidents Cup win since 1998. "They [the crowd] took a while to warm their voice, Chicago, but they got there today.

"I thought they should be yelling for their team - they shouldn't be yelling in swings. I didn't hear too much of that, but I'm sure it happened and it sounds like it's happened a little bit.

"When you've got a national team or your team, gaining momentum on a day like that and this many people and hearing cheers everywhere, it's contagious - it grows and it builds. That's just the nature of being crowds.

"I would hope that we wouldn't have any stories like Nico's [Echavarria] in Australia [2028], but you can't guarantee anything. Like I said, it's momentum of a crowd when they get excited. They should get excited - their home team was turning it around."

The United States will be back in action next September when they take on Team Europe in the Ryder Cup, held at Adare Manor in Ireland from September 17-19. The next Presidents Cup will be held in 2028 at Kingston Heath Golf Club in Melbourne, Australia.

articles.title: United States rallies to capture dramatic Presidents Cup over International team
articles.summary: The United States mounted an impressive comeback to win the Presidents Cup on Sunday.
articles.body:
For most of its existence, the Presidents Cup has been a junior varsity version of the Ryder Cup, uncompetitive — the United States had a 13-1-1 record against International players prior to this year — and, for the most part, unremarkable.

That all changed this year. An International squad outmatched statistically overwhelmed the United States on the fairways and greens of Medinah Country Club, and what had been a sleepwalk for the United States for virtually the entire century suddenly became a fight for every single point all the way down to the final matches. The United States claimed 15.5 points to win the Cup with two matches still on the course, and won the event by a final score of 17-13.

The Presidents Cup Sunday matches included everything from dramatic clinching shots to an exceptional display of sportsmanship , and in the end, the event justified itself — in large part because the United States can no longer take the Presidents Cup for granted.

Regardless of the result, the United States is now in the grips of a full-blown match play crisis following its humiliating team performances earlier in the week. Between this week and last year's Ryder Cup implosion, the United States appears to have no clue at all of how to win team match play reliably, despite having most of the best players in the world on its roster.

With less than a year waiting until the Ryder Cup, the United States has little time to fix its many team match play problems. "They just putted better" isn't an excuse for struggling on your home greens, and the difficulties of stars like Scottie Scheffler in match play aren't the kind of problems that solve themselves. The earth has shifted under the United States' feet, and the Americans need to figure out how to steady themselves if they'll ever regain their past dominance.

But for the moment, the United States can revel in this victory, which came about through individual resilience and strong rookie performances. That's a good place for the Americans to start to build a new team foundation.

Early sessions: The Internationals take charge

Coming into the week, there was little indication that the International Team would be any more competitive this year than they've been since 1998, the last (and only) time they'd won this event outright. Eight of the top 11 players in the Official World Golf Rankings are on the American roster. J.J. Spaun, left at home by team captain Brandt Snedeker, would have been the highest-ranked player on the International team. Si Woo Kim, at No. 14, is the Internationals' highest-ranked player.

And yet, when team match play begins, none of those individual rankings seem to matter a bit. The United States won the Thursday fourballs session , taking three matches to the Internationals' two, a respectable but not dominating performance in the better-ball event.

"We just did our best to stay in it," Scottie Scheffler said after wrangling a 1-up win with Sam Burns over Min Woo Lee and Sungjae Im. "I felt like both teams got off to pretty hot starts today and we cooled off a little bit off that."

On Friday, though, the United States' wheels came off. In foursomes, where the players must alternate shots on the same ball, the Internationals thoroughly dominated, winning all five of the day's sessions. That gave the Internationals a solid 7-3 cushion heading into Saturday.

"You're going to have sessions like this in these things," Snedeker said afterward. "I feel terrible for the guys because I know they grinded out there and gave me everything they had today, and it wasn't meant to be."

Given a chance to close the gap again in a fourball session, the United States could only manage 2.5 points out of 4, narrowing their deficit by just a single point to 8.5-5.5. And then came the second fourball session, which turned out to be a devastating blow to the United States' hopes.

The Americans, at one point, led in all four foursomes matches; if they'd held their lead, they would have entered Sunday with a one-point lead. But the United States let two of the matches slip through their fingers, and as a result trailed by three points after three days , 10.5-7.5.

Snedeker made the debatable decision to bench Scheffler — who has a 1-8-1 record in team foursomes but remains the world's best golfer — on Saturday afternoon. But Snedeker had nothing to do with the way the United States surrendered its control of the foursomes on Saturday afternoon.

Sam Burns and Wyndham Clark posted an early 2-up lead over Ryan Fox and Lee, and were tied as late as the 12th hole, before falling 3 and 2. Russell Henley and Jacob Bridgeman held 3-up leads two different times, including as late as the 10th hole, before Corey Conners and Nick Taylor went on a tear and birdied four of the next five holes to win 1-up. Even a halve by Henley and Bridgeman would have helped tighten the overall gap to two points.

"I've just got to figure out ways to get these guys in better situations," Snedeker said Saturday evening. "I don't think I've held up my end of the bargain. The guys have done everything I've asked of them so far. I think we've got a great match for [Sunday]. I think we've got a great lineup here. I'm excited about what the guys can bring [Sunday]."

Sunday singles: The United States' last chance

Sunday marked the first time that the Internationals had held a lead on United States soil. With the score at 10.5-7.5, the Internationals needed just five points from the 12 matches, while the United States needed to win eight total points to hold onto the cup.

A fiery, partisan gallery greeted the players from the day's opening tee shots. The United States spent much of the day with red up and down the in-progress leaderboard, but the challenge for the Americans all week wasn't starting, it was finishing. Cam Young notched the United States' first point of Sunday, rallying from a 2-down deficit to defeat Ryo Hisatsune 3&2 in the lead singles match.

Justin Thomas notched the second United States point, knocking off Conners 5&3, but shortly afterward, Tom Kim picked up the first International point of the day by beating Wyndham Clark 3&2.

Mindful of the way that the Bethpage Black's galleries wrecked the entire image of the Ryder Cup, Scheffler conceded the 14th hole to Nico Echavarria after a fan shouted in Echavarria's backswing.

Echavarria made it interesting with a miraculous chip on 16, but Scheffler closed him out on the 17th green to draw the United States within a point of the Internationals, and within five points of retaining the Cup. Soon afterward, Im knocked off Sam Burns 3&1, giving the Internationals a bit more breathing room as the day grew late.

Slowly, inexorably, the United States' talent began to assert itself. With eight groups remaining on the course and all within the final six holes, the United States' red obliterated the Internationals' gold on the scoreboard. The best example of the United States' vibe reversal: Patrick Cantlay's 57-foot putt to keep the pressure on Adam Scott:

Nearly two hours after Young put the day's first point on the board for the United States, Chris Gotterup finally dispatched Christiaan Bezuidenhout to claim another and pull within a single point of the Internationals and four points away from victory. Cantlay followed up with a win over Scott to tie the match, and seconds later, Collin Morikawa dispatched Hideki Matsuyama in the day's most entertaining back-and-forth match. That left the United States one point ahead, 13.5 to 12.5, and just two points away from retaining the Cup.

In the final slot, Xander Schauffele spent the afternoon decimating fellow Open champion Ryan Fox, meaning that the Internationals needed to win all three of the remaining matches outright. Jackson Koivun, the 21-year-old who was playing for Auburn just a few months ago, virtually eliminated that possibility when he closed out Si Woo Kim to move the United States to 14.5 points.

The winning putt fell to rookie Jacob Bridgeman, who closed out Lee on the 18th green:

The United States claimed the Cup, but the questions for the larger American team golf effort remain.

articles.summary: The United States snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, coming from behind on the final day to beat the International team 17-13.
articles.body:
The United States snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, coming from behind on the final day to beat the International team 17-13.

The U.S. trailed by three points after Saturday, but singles play has traditionally been where the Americans thrived in team tournaments. That once again proved true at Medinah Country Club.

The Internationals lost nine of the 12 head-to-head battles.

Cameron Young gave the United States an ideal start by cruising past Ryo Hisatsune. Hisatsune was 2-up midway through the front nine, but Young tied things up before they made the turn.

The reigning Players Championship winner found another gear on the back nine, winning Nos. 11, 12 and 13 to take a commanding lead, and eventually closed out the match on the 16th hole.

Justin Thomas was even more dominant in his match with Corey Conners. The two-time major champion took the first hole and never trailed. He was 5-up through six, and that proved to be his margin of victory.

Scottie Scheffler lived up to the billing as well. The No. 1 player in the world was up four holes on Nico Echavarria shortly after making the turn. Echavarria tried to keep things interesting by winning No. 16 but had too much ground to make up in too little time.

His birdie chip on the 16th hole was at least something worth appreciating:

The International team kept up the pressure with points from Tom Kim and Sungjae Im.

That did little to dent the United States' wider momentum, though. The Americans were in the driver's seat for the majority of the remaining matches.

Si Woo Kim summed up the day for the Internationals. He got up on Jackson Koivun early in the round and led by two through 10 holes.

As the pressure ratcheted up, however, the far more experienced Kim started to crack. Koivun, who only turned pro in June, displayed a ton of poise by winning four holes over a five-hole stretch to turn the tables on Kim.

Hideki Matsuyama was also unable to seal the deal against Collin Morikawa. Matsuyama was 1-up through 14 before Morikawa birdied No. 15 to tie the match. They went shot-for-shot on No. 16 and 17 before Morikawa's birdie on the 18th hole secured a crucial point for the U.S.

With Xander Schauffele holding a sizable advantage on Ryan Fox, the math was working against the Internationals. A Schauffele win was enough to get the United States to the magic number of 15 points.

Jacob Bridgeman stole his thunder by sinking a par putt on No. 18 to beat Min Woo Lee.

A loss to the Internationals would've been a disaster for the United States.

The U.S. has dominated the Presidents Cup, losing just one of the first 15 events since its inception in 1994. This year's team had the added pressure of salvaging some of the United States' honor amid a brutal run in team tourneys.

That started with the 2025 Ryder Cup, where a final-day flurry wasn't enough to avoid a 15-13 loss on home soil. Then this year, the Curtis Cup, Walker Cup and Solheim Cup all slipped through the Americans' grasp.

The recriminations would've reached a fever pitch if the Presidents Cup made it a complete sweep for Europe and the rest of the world.

In one sense, the United States' comeback might be bad in the bigger picture because it potentially allows U.S. golf power brokers to avoid addressing the country's continued failings in fourballs and foursomes.

Whether it's Europe in the Ryder Cup or the Internationals in the Presidents Cup, the United States' opponents continually display more chemistry and cohesion.

Figuring out a formula to remedy this trend is the challenge that lays before 2027 Ryder Cup captain Jim Furyk.

The U.S. hasn't won a Ryder Cup on foreign soil since 1993, so Europe will be the favorite when play opens next year at Adare Manor. Maybe 2025 and 2026 served as a wakeup call for the best American golfers to at least make the next Ryder Cup more competitive on the first two days.

articles.title: United States complete thrilling comeback to retain Presidents Cup
articles.summary: The United States complete a thrilling comeback on the final day to beat the Internationals and win an 11th successive Presidents Cup.
articles.body:
The United States completed a thrilling comeback on the final day to beat the Internationals and win an 11th successive Presidents Cup.

The hosts, containing eight of the world's 11 top-ranked players, trailed by three points going into Sunday and were looking to avoid just a second defeat since the biennial competition began 32 years ago.

They dominated the singles, winning nine of the 12 matches, to seal a 17-13 win at Medinah - the scene of Team Europe's famous Ryder Cup comeback win in 2012.

Jacob Bridgeman secured the decisive point by holing a four-foot par putt at the 18th to seal a one-up win over Australia's Min Woo Lee.

There were also wins for Cameron Young, Justin Thomas, Scottie Scheffler, Chris Gotterup, Collin Morikawa, Patrick Cantlay, Xander Schauffele and Jackson Koivun.

"I told the guys last night that funny stuff happens here. Medinah's got a history of funny things happening," said US captain Brandt Snedeker, who was a member of the team beaten by Europe in 2012.

"All these guys fought for each other, fought for this country, fought for this team."

International captain Geoff Ogilvy said: "The US team came out firing, we knew they would.

"It was on a knife edge all day. If some of those one downs we had out there had flipped to one up, the numbers looked really good and who knows what momentum that could give."

US President Donald Trump was in attendance in his role as honorary chairman, greeting the players and making a speech before the matches got under way.

articles.title: Presidents Cup: Team USA beat International Team 17-13 after epic Sunday singles fightback to avoid shock Medinah loss
articles.summary: Jacob Bridgeman claimed the winning point for Team USA, who dominated the Sunday singles to complete a dramatic Presidents Cup comeback at Medinah; Brandt Snedeker's side won 9.5 points during the final day to continue their dominance against the International Team
articles.body:
Brandt Snedeker's trailed by three points heading into the Sunday singles at Medinah, leaving Team USA requiring eight points from the final 12 matches to avoid a first defeat since 1998, but responded in spectacular fashion.

Cameron Young, Justin Thomas and Scottie Scheffler all delivered points early for Team USA, only for Tom Kim and Sungjae Im to register key wins to move the Internationals within three points of a first away win in the biennial contest.

Wins for Chris Gotterup, Patrick Cantlay and Collin Morikawa pushed the United States ahead, while Jackson Koivun's point - as Xander Schauffele already had a dormie half guaranteed against Ryan Fox - ended the Internationals' hopes of victory.

Jacob Bridgeman earned the point to guarantee Team USA would lift the trophy again, coming back from one down with three to play to defeat Min Woo Lee on the final hole, completing the biggest final-day comeback in Presidents Cup history and sparking wild celebrations.

Xander Schauffele beat Open champion Ryan Fox 2&1 to extend the winning margin, while Russell Henley's tied match with Nick Taylor left Team USA with a record 9.5 points from the singles session.

Team USA continue their record of winning every edition of the Presidents Cup since 2005, while a disappointing final day from Geoff Ogilvy's International Team extends their wait for an elusive second victory and first on American soil.

How Team USA snatched Presidents Cup thriller

Young delivered in the top match for Team USA, just as he did when sent out first at the Ryder Cup last September, as he recovered from falling two behind early against rookie Ryo Hisatsune to win three consecutive holes after the turn and take control.

The Players champion rolled in from 30 feet at the par-three 16th to close a 3&2 win and earn their first point, with Thomas following soon after winning five of the first six holes in his 5&3 victory over Corey Conners.

Kim fell behind early against Wyndham Clark but made three birdies in a four-hole stretch around the turn, with the Korean beating the US Open champion 3&2 to secure his fourth point of the week and offer hope to the Internationals.

Im also beat Sam Burns to leave Geoff Ogilvy's side closer to victory, but Scheffler quickly closed the advantage as the leaderboard turned increasingly red.

Scheffler never trailed against Nico Echavarria and raced into a four-hole advantage, only to be left angered by a spectator yelling in his opponent's backswing at the par-four 14th.

The world No 1 generously conceded a 32-foot par for Echavarria, who chipped in from off the 16th green to extend the match until Scheffler completed victory to finish as the United States' joint-top scorer.

Gotterup edged a final-hole win over Christiaan Bezuidenhout and Cantlay holed an incredible 57-foot birdie at the 16th to help close out a 2&1 win over Adam Scott, levelling the contest with five matches on the course.

Morikawa capitalised on a final-hole bogey from Hideki Matsuyama to grab a 1up win, as Koivun - the only unbeaten American player this week - came back from two down to birdie three of his last seven holes and earn a 2up victory over Si Woo Kim.

Schauffele looked destined to secure the winning point but lost back-to-back holes late in his 2&1 win over Ryan Fox, allowing Bridgeman - on debut - to push Team USA to their winning target with his victory over Lee.

The United States will be back in action next September when they take on Team Europe in the Ryder Cup, held at Adare Manor in Ireland from September 17-19. The next Presidents Cup will be held in 2028 at Kingston Heath Golf Club in Melbourne, Australia.

articles.title: Trump gets credit for U.S. Presidents Cup win at trophy ceremony
articles.summary: The United States authored a stirring comeback to win the 2026 Presidents Cup and President Donald Trump was there to celebrate with them.
articles.body:
MEDINAH, IL — The United States authored a stirring comeback to win the 2026 Presidents Cup and President Donald Trump was there to celebrate with them.

Trump, in his role as honorary chairman, presented the Americans with the Presidents Cup trophy after arriving with his motorcade on the 14th green in front of the Byzantine-style clubhouse at Medinah Country Club soon after the U.S. clinched its 11th consecutive victory at golf's biennial global team match-play event.

The U.S. won nine of the 12 singles matches on Sunday to come from behind to prevail. Afterwards, U.S. team captain Brandt Snedeker praised Trump's presence for helping provide motivation for the final-day charge.

Final round at Medinah delivers tense moments for Presidents Cup

"It's really special because I got to meet President Trump today on the first tee," Snedeker said as Trump watched on with PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp. "As he told me this morning, he brought some juice for us today and I told him if it turned out our way, I was going to give him credit. He definitely brought the juice. He deserves a lot of the credit for what happened today."

Trump shook hands and congratulated every U.S. golfer and vice-captain on the team before handing Snedeker the trophy.

About eight hours earlier, Trump also gave brief remarks before the start of the final day at the 2026 Presidents Cup. After being introduced by Rolapp, Trump joked he wasn't brave enough to subject the crowd to a speech. He then jabbed at the "fake news media," whom he said would report that he received a poor reception.

"Brian said could you make a short speech and I said, 'No, I don't have the courage to make a speech. These people want to see golf. They don't want to hear speeches,'" Trump said to the crowd about 30 minutes before the first match teed off. "I will say this, our country is doing great, better than ever before. And now I want to watch the greatest players in the world go at it today and play your hearts out. It should be a very impressive day of golf."

Trump then greeted all the golfers from both the U.S. and International teams before each player teed off on the first hole, which features a grandstand that can accommodate as many as 5,000 people. Fans filled the bleachers and lined the first fairway for the initial groups for Trump's first visit to the Chicago area during his second term in the White House and the final day of golf's biennial global match-play event.

PGA Tour officials announced enhanced security and additional restrictions at Medinah outside Chicago for Trump's visit. It included TSA-style security screening to enter the first tee grandstand. His presence also led to a temporary ground stop for departures at nearby O'Hare International Airport being issued due to "VIP," the Federal Aviation Administration said. Air Force One could be seen flying over Medinah shortly after gates opened on Sunday morning.

Trump was named the honorary chairman of the Presidents Cup last month and announced he would be on hand for the event. It's the second time he's served as honorary chairman for the tournament, having previously hosted it during his first term at his Liberty National Golf Club in New Jersey in 2017.

There have been six other U.S. presidents to hold the role of honorary chairman at the Presidents Cup: Joe Biden, Barack Obama, George W. Bush, Bill Clinton, George H.W. Bush and Gerald Ford.

articles.title: My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die
articles.summary: Aberdeen is launching an ambitious bid to revive its struggling centre. Could it offer lessons for other high streets?
articles.body:
The empty building that used to be the home of Marks & Spencer in Aberdeen is one of the first things you see when you arrive off the train and come into the city centre. The sign has gone, though the shape of the lettering can still be made out; the windows are blacked out and the doors boarded up.

This is my hometown. As a teenager, I spent hours on Union Street, its main thoroughfare, nicknamed the Granite Mile after the local silver-grey stone. It was the place to try on all the latest fashions from the likes of Clockhouse and Chelsea Girl.

The street used to be packed with shoppers from across the north-east of Scotland.

"I come to Union Street to take a bus somewhere else... there's nothing to shop for now… it's horrendous," complains Marie Sim, a lifelong Aberdeen resident.

It's a similar story across the country: High Streets, once bursting with shops, hit first by the rise of out-of-town retail centres and then by online commerce.

But Aberdeen is in the thick of an ambitious turnaround plan. The port city has essentially declared war on its empty shop problem, taking an unusually hands-on approach to filling vacant units and bringing long-neglected upper floors of buildings into use.

On top of that, the council is pouring tens of millions into trying to make the city centre a destination again. Like many other places, it's leaning into the "experience economy", with a new indoor food and drink market and a major redevelopment of the seafront.

High Streets are integral to how we feel about where we live. The sight of vacant shops and graffiti can quickly become a vicious circle, deterring shoppers, discouraging investment and leading to anti-social behaviour.

Politicians of all stripes have been trying for years to breathe new life into town centres - and Andy Burnham, who has made a focus on "place" part of his political identity, is the latest. He argues they should become "symbols of Britain's renaissance".

But can it be achieved? And if they're to survive, do town centres need a fundamental rethink?

One in eight properties on British High Streets are currently vacant, according to Green Street, the property and retail analytics company, a number that's stayed stubbornly high for years.

"If there was a silver bullet, it would have been fired years ago," says Jackie Sadek, a former government adviser on urban regeneration, who has spent nearly four decades working in town centre renewal.

One of the biggest obstacles is fractured ownership. Shops and buildings are often owned by dozens of different landlords, sometimes through offshore companies or complex structures, each with their own interests and priorities. That can slow decision-making and make large-scale regeneration difficult.

But even with empty units that are available, you need to find someone willing to take them on.

Many units are old and need modernising.

The cost of running a High Street business has also risen; employment costs are higher, and there's the burden of business rates.

Firms need customers. Footfall on many High Streets has been in long-term decline as shopping and services move online, and this enormous structural shift has yet to play out fully.

Two-thirds of town centre experts think there is still 20% to 40% too much retail space, according to a survey by retail body Revo and real estate consultancy Lambert Smith Hampton.

In Aberdeen's boom years of North Sea oil, from the late 1970s through to the early 2010s, it didn't have to work hard to fill its hotels and restaurants and get the cash tills ringing because of the wealth the energy industry brought to the city.

I remember weekends with friends as a teenager, spending whatever cash we had in the fashion chains and shoe shops. Later came the pubs and bar-hopping, and trips to the art deco Capitol Theatre (now office space), where I saw Duran Duran.

But by the end of 2022, Union Street had hit rock bottom. Aberdonians had long deserted the High Street for a shopping centre, which opened in 2009 next to the railway station.

"They'd fallen out of love with their city," says Bob Keiller, head of Our Union Street coalition, a community-led group formed after an emergency summit to reverse the decline.

The first thing it did was listen to what residents wanted, receiving thousands of submissions. Restoring a bit of civic pride and filling empty units became the focus.

It's been a co-ordinated effort, involving letting agents, the council, landlords, businesses and a big team of volunteers, led by Keiller, a former FTSE 100 CEO, who isn't getting paid. He has a map on his office wall, detailing the status of every property, unit by unit, with colour-coded Post-it notes.

They audited the street, tracking down absent landlords, and logging what was empty and why. Volunteers offered to give the empty properties a clean and a lick of paint, to make them more attractive to let. They also spruced up the streets, picking litter, weeding, and painting bins. A small team still goes out once a fortnight.

There's a website where all the available properties are collated; crucially, all of the financial incentives are also listed. These can include council fit-out grants (where a new business gets money to decorate premises), and a two-year discount from business rates.

In 2023, 57 of the 198 units on Union Street were empty. As of today, 33 have been filled, with a further 14 in the process of being let.

But it can feel like a game of whack-a-mole because since the initiative started, another 20 units have become vacant. "The key thing is, we're filling quicker than emptying," Keiller insists.

Keiller's operations director, David McKeith, describes it as putting an arm round the shoulder of those they can help and being a "wasp in the ear" of people who just say no.

At one end of the office, a small, young team produces social media content, linking visitors and residents to a new Our Aberdeen app, showing what the city can offer.

For Keiller, the "small wins" - like tackling graffiti - are needed to help change public perception.

"We've realised the psychology is not to do it once but be prepared to do it two or three times before people that do these things eventually say, 'there's no point in putting it there because somebody's going to paint over it.'"

Attention is also turning to the often-forgotten upper floors of buildings along the once-iconic Union Street. In a separate initiative, experts are getting inside those vacant high-up spaces to identify the barriers to bringing them back into use.

Aberdeen sought the help of a High Street troubleshooter, Iain Nicholson, who's worked with dozens of towns and cities through his Vacant Shops Academy.

Out of more than 1,000 empty units he helped audit nationally, on average more than half didn't have a letting agent actively marketing the property. He says some councils don't even know who the landlords are.

Empty shops, he says, won't all be filled by the market alone. Towns and cities need to encourage a broader range of occupiers, from arts and culture to leisure, health and well-being.

He says what's striking about Aberdeen is its joined-up approach, and the fact people "rolled up their sleeves" and overcame differences. "That's not something you can yet say about everywhere."

Every town and city faces its own mix of challenges.

Nicholson also helped Crewe in Cheshire. As a smaller place than Aberdeen, it is focusing on arts, culture, and community, with a new women's centre opened this month.

And English councils are being encouraged to take a more interventionist role.

They can now force an empty commercial unit that's been vacant for at least a year to be offered to tenants through a High Street Rental Auction, even if the landlord doesn't want to let it.

It's early days but the mere prospect of losing control of a property is delivering some results. Bassetlaw Council in Nottinghamshire, an early adopter of the scheme, says more than 30 shops across the district have been let or are currently under offer as a result of the policy.

But filling empty units is only part of the challenge. The bigger question is what town and city centres are actually for.

Changing habits mean we won't need so many shops. Instead, it's argued, town centres will need more people living and working in them, with new homes and office space alongside services that can't be done online. With an ageing population, for example, bringing NHS health centres into the heart of a town could be a big opportunity.

In Aberdeen, the building that used to house BHS - a department store shuttered in 2016 - is being converted into an entrance plaza for the new food and drink market.

The physical appearance of Union Street is changing too. Like many Victorian shopping thoroughfares, it was built with a wide road (probably to give space to horses and carriages). Now parts of the pavements are being widened to make it a more pleasant place to spend time, though many Aberdonians are weary of the disruption, and of new traffic restrictions.

Money is a big barrier. Aberdeen's new indoor food and drink market is costing £40m, funded by the council and the UK Levelling Up Fund. In other places, regeneration schemes can struggle because the cost of redevelopment outweighs the likely financial return, making support from the public sector essential. And the economics are becoming more challenging.

"Higher interest rates, rising costs of construction and other issues are impacting the viability and delivery of new housing and big redevelopment projects," says Steve Norris, a director at Lambert Smith Hampton. He says that big projects usually require cash from both the public and private sectors.

He wants to see "more creative ways of funding".

Part of Burnham's plan is to give local leaders more freedom to invest in town centres and drive regeneration, building on the approach he has championed in Greater Manchester. But bigger projects take years.

Making it easier and cheaper to open and run a High Street business is one of the more immediate solutions being called for, with business rates a particular concern.

Burnham has promised further rates reform. All eyes are on this month's Budget to see how far he will go.

The chief executive of Next, Simon Wolfson, argues that the bigger challenge is not business rates, but planning reform.

"The most important thing that the government can do for high streets is let them develop," says Wolfson, who's also a Conservative peer.

Back in Aberdeen, there are some signs of traction.

Lauren Reid and her mother Rose moved their fashion boutique to Union Street in 2024. A council grant helped with the refurbishment after they decided to make the leap.

Can they make the sums add up? "We're getting there," she says.

She feels the same about the future of her street. "I always say Rome wasn't built in a day."

Right now the area feels like a construction site - but another gaping hole will soon be filled. Robert Keane is a local property developer who in 2023 bought the Trinity shopping centre, once home to Debenhams. The space is now set to be re-occupied by a national leisure brand. A notoriously tiring stairway leading to the Trinity from the train station is also being replaced by an escalator.

"We saw a real good opportunity, because it was dying," he says.

He reckons he can make a go of it, cutting the cost of parking and overheads, resetting rents and being more nimble than previous far-flung owners.

It was a bold move given Lambert Smith Hampton suggests that more than one in 10 UK shopping centres is ripe for demolition.

But he's betting the dynamics of Aberdeen are finally changing.

"I think by 2027 it should look and feel like a different city."

That is certainly the hope. Yet walking along Union Street today, past the boarded-up shopfronts and roadworks, it can still feel like a city caught between its past and whatever comes next.

articles.title: Team USA captain thanks Trump after massive Presidents Cup comeback: ‘He gets all the credit’
articles.summary: Trump told captain Brandt Snedeker he'd bring energy to the Presidents Cup, and the U.S. rallied from a three-point deficit in Sunday singles.
articles.body: U.S. captain Brandt Snedeker credited President Donald Trump after the Americans rallied for a 17-13 victory over the International team at the Presidents Cup on Sunday. "One last shoutout: Donald Trump. President Trump. He told me, 'I [am] going to bring energy today for you. You guys need it,'" Snedeker said. "I told him if we did this, he gets all the credit. So, thank you, President Trump." With Trump in attendance, the United States team found itself in uncharted territory heading into Sunday singles at Medinah Country Club. For the first time in the event's history, Team USA trailed on home soil entering the final session. TEAM USA GOLFERS WELCOME TRUMP’S EXPECTED PRESIDENTS CUP VISIT, SHARE PRIDE IN REPRESENTING AMERICA Trump, the event's honorary chairman, briefly addressed the crowd from the first tee before play began. "You know, the fake news media will say I get a very bad reception," Trump said as the crowd laughed. "But we get a good reception." "[PGA Tour CEO] Brian [Rolapp] said, 'Could you make a short speech?' I said, 'No, I don't have the courage to make a speech. These people wanna see golf. They don't wanna hear speeches.' I'll only say this: Our country is doing great, better than ever before." The Americans entered the week having won all eight Presidents Cups played on home soil and 10 straight overall. But Team USA was also coming off a 15-13 loss to Europe at last year's Ryder Cup at Bethpage Black. The last thing American golf needed was another visiting team celebrating a victory on U.S. soil. Instead, the Americans erased a 10½-7½ deficit by winning nine of the 12 singles matches and outscoring the Internationals 9½-2½. Presidents Cup rookie Jacob Bridgeman delivered the winning point with a par putt on the 18th green. USA sent an early message on Sunday Snedeker sent out some of his best players in the first few matches, hoping to swing the event and put pressure on the Internationals. Cameron Young led off, with Justin Thomas and Scottie Scheffler going out third and fourth. The plan worked. Young did his job as the leadoff man, despite falling 2 down to Ryo Hisatsune after four holes. He won five of the next 12 holes to close out a 3&2 victory. Match play specialist Justin Thomas, who entered Sunday with a 20-10-5 career record in Ryder Cups and Presidents Cups, won five of the first six holes against Corey Conners before coasting to a 5&3 win. Nico Echavarria gave Scheffler a little more trouble than many might have expected, but the world's No. 1 player ultimately closed out the 32-year-old Colombian, 2&1. However, the International team wasn't going down easily. Tom Kim capped an incredible week by beating world No. 5 Wyndham Clark, finishing as the tournament's leading scorer with four points. Sungjae Im also took down world No. 8 Sam Burns. Chris Gotterup was a major bright spot for the Americans all tournament. The 27-year-old Presidents Cup rookie defeated Christiaan Bezuidenhout 1 up and finished 3-1 for the week. He made a strong case for a spot on the 2027 Ryder Cup team in the process. US PRESIDENTS CUP PLAYERS EXPLAIN HOW CHRISTIAN FAITH BUILDS FRIENDSHIPS AND PUTS GOLF IN PERSPECTIVE Arguably the best match of the day featured Collin Morikawa and Japan's Hideki Matsuyama. Matsuyama jumped out to a 2-up lead through six holes, but Morikawa battled back and took the lead by winning the 10th. Matsuyama won two straight holes to move back in front, only for Morikawa to square the match again at 15. The pair tied 16 and 17, sending them to the 18th all square. On 18, Matsuyama drove into the rough and could only advance his second shot short of the green. His pitch ran 15 feet past the hole, while Morikawa cozied a long birdie putt to within 2½ feet. Matsuyama missed his par putt, giving Morikawa a 1-up win and the Americans a much-needed full point. Cantlay makes a major statement Patrick Cantlay delivered one of the afternoon's biggest moments in his match against Adam Scott, burying a 57-foot birdie putt from just off the 16th green. The usually reserved Cantlay pumped his fist hard and yelled, "YES! YES!" to the crowd, which was going wild, sensing the gravity of the moment. Cantlay closed out Scott on 17, 2&1. His victory and Morikawa's came moments apart, putting the U.S. ahead 13½-12½ with four matches still on the course. With Xander Schauffele holding a commanding lead, the Americans looked set for another point. That put the pressure on rookies Jackson Koivun and Bridgeman, along with the steady veteran Russell Henley, to finish the comeback. Koivun, a 21-year-old Presidents Cup rookie, was 2 down at the turn against Si Woo Kim, who entered Sunday tied for the tournament lead with three points. But Koivun completely flipped the match on the back nine, winning holes 11, 12, 13 and 15. Koivun took a 1-up lead to 18, where Kim hit his approach to 15 feet. But the rookie wasn't intimidated. After driving it down the middle of the fairway, the Auburn product stuck his approach to eight feet. Kim lipped out his birdie putt, and Koivun secured another crucial point to push the U.S. total to 14½. CANADIANS NICK TAYLOR AND COREY CONNERS LAUGH OFF LAKE ONTARIO RENAMING AHEAD OF PRESIDENTS CUP Bridgeman delivered another clutch moment from an American rookie, burying an eight-foot par putt on 16. Min Woo Lee missed his four-footer for par, squaring their match with two holes to play. With Schauffele guaranteed at least a half-point, the Americans could do no worse than a tie and needed just another half-point beyond that to win the Cup outright. Schauffele had been 4 up with four holes to play, but lost 15 and 16, keeping the Americans waiting a little longer. Apparently, the afternoon hadn't been dramatic enough. Schauffele's delay left the honor to Bridgeman. Fittingly, the rookie delivered, sinking his par putt on 18 to beat Lee 1 up and give the Americans the 15½ points they needed. A "U-S-A!" chant broke out from the crowd as Bridgeman's putt dropped, and the Americans celebrated on the 18th green. Schauffele eventually closed out Ryan Fox, 2&1, while Henley halved his match with Nick Taylor to complete the 17-13 victory. The win was the Americans' 11th straight in the Presidents Cup and ninth in nine tries at home, improving their overall record to 14-1-1. USA still has work to do before the Ryder Cup Of course, the Americans never should have put themselves in this position. Eight U.S. players entered the week ranked higher than Si Woo Kim, the International team's highest-ranked player at No. 14. Seven Americans were inside the world's top 10. The visitors didn't have one. At home, against that roster, this should have been a blowout. It certainly shouldn't have required a three-point comeback on Sunday. Instead, the International team swept Friday's foursomes 5-0, just as it did at Royal Montreal in 2024. That turned a 3-2 U.S. lead after Thursday into a 7-3 deficit heading into Saturday. Saturday offered opportunities to regain control. The Americans led all four matches at one point in each of the day's two sessions, but finished with just a 4½-3½ edge. That still left them down three entering Sunday. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Clark finished 1-4 for the week, while Henley went winless in three matches, earning just a half-point. That followed last year's embarrassing Ryder Cup loss at Bethpage Black. And the next Ryder Cup sends Team USA to Adare Manor in Ireland in 2027, tasked with doing something the Americans haven't done since 1993: winning on European soil. Sunday singles should give the Americans some confidence heading to Ireland. They won that session 7½-4½ at the 2024 Presidents Cup and 8½-3½ at last year's Ryder Cup before hammering the Internationals 9½-2½ at Medinah. But Bethpage already showed that even a great Sunday might not be enough. Team USA needs to clean up its play in the team formats, particularly foursomes, and stop leaving itself so much work to do on the final day.

articles.title: Former Lakers Champion Says Austin Reaves Prevent Success
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Lakers have a tough task of finding a path towards NBA Championship contention in the stacked Western Conference. Luka Doncic leading the tea...
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers have a tough task of finding a path towards NBA Championship contention in the stacked Western Conference. Luka Doncic leading the team is a huge positive, but they have to find ways to contend against elite teams like the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder . Former NBA Champion Danny Green went out of his way to name Austin Reaves for why he feels the Lakers can't win.

Green was part of the 2020 Lakers Championship and revealed why he thinks Reaves will hold them back:

"I don't think he is a No. 2. In today's NBA, I think he's a No. 3… In today's league, your big has to be either one or two because of how [Nikola] Jokic , [ Victor Wembanyama ], Joel [Embiid]…those guys that you have to match up with. And your guards, [ Shai Gilgeous-Alexander ], [Jalen] Brunson , like you need your No. 1 to be either one of those guys and No. 2, one of those guys on the wing."

Green listed the other top stars and how all of them have better "number two" fits than Doncic and Reaves. Teams like the Thunder, Spurs, New York Knicks , and Denver Nuggets all have better roster dynamics. Lakers fans are hoping that Green is wrong and that Reaves can be a top two player on a title contender.

Why Danny Green Called Out Austin Reaves

The Lakers roster construction is risky with Reaves and Walker Kessler unproven in the roles needed. Reaves received a major contract to be the second star behind Doncic after his incredible improvement last season.

Losing LeBron James already put the odds against the Lakers after he played All-Star level basketball. Reaves is going to have to put up 25 points per game and improve at other areas of the game like defense and facilitating.

The Lakers extended Reaves due to their belief in him, but Green and other pundits don't have that same faith. General Manager Rob Pelinka put his future on the line by investing in Reaves and Kessler as cornerstone behind Doncic. Reaves must prove Pelinka right and all his critics wrong for this Lakers roster to work.

If the Lakers fail to contend this season, Reaves will likely be the first name gone due to the roster. Pelinka trading the last two valued draft picks to the Utah Jazz for Kessler makes it hard for them to acquire noteworthy talents via trade.

This roster failing will see a Reaves trade for an older and more proven star. Kyrie Irving was one name rumored down the line , but a lot of other variables must occur, including the Dallas Mavericks looking to get younger.

Reaves is the perfect age for rebuilding teams to take a chance on in a potential trade, like the Brooklyn Nets or Milwaukee Bucks . The Lakers will either thrive with this roster or must move on from Reaves to add centers or wing players. Green is betting on his championship experience revealing that Doncic and Reaves can't win together.
